summary: The note examines the legal fallout from a series of internet outages beginning September 5, 2023, which combined a DDoS attack on MyNet Co. and a fiber cut in Metropolis City. It covers the impact on workers and businesses, SLA and force majeure disputes, a class-action lawsuit, regulatory responses, a High Court ruling, the debate over treating the internet as a public utility, and corporate damage control.
one_line: Legal and regulatory consequences of the September 2023 internet outages, including MyNet Co.'s DDoS attack, a class action, and a High Court ruling.
key_facts: Outages began on September 5, 2023, caused by a mix of technical failures and cyber attacks.
MyNet Co., a major internet service provider, suffered a massive DDoS attack traced to an unidentified non-state actor, causing an outage of about six hours on September 7.

A large-scale fiber cut, reportedly from a construction mishap in downtown Metropolis City, worsened the situation the following day and affected subscribers, businesses, hospitals and government agencies.
Freelance graphic designer Sarah Johnson said on September 12 that she missed client deadlines and that compensation for the interruption is not covered in her contract.

Under most SLAs, internet providers commit to uptime of typically around 99.9% availability, but force majeure clauses often exonerate them for unforeseeable circumstances such as natural disasters or third-party actions.
On September 18, a class-action lawsuit was filed against MyNet Co. by a coalition of small business owners, including a group led by Elena Gomez, owner of a local bookstore chain.
On September 24, the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) hinted at reevaluating policies and possibly setting minimum redundancy standards for critical provider infrastructure.
Robert Carter of the Consumer Rights Protection Bureau reported a high volume of complaints following the outages.
On September 28, the High Court under Judge Maria Lopez ruled that prolonged interruption of internet services 'constitutes a breach of the fundamental right to information.'
Lawyer Jonathan Reed argued that users are not without recourse and that prolonged outages represent a failure to deliver on a paid service.
The European Union has pursued a 'digital single market' prioritizing uninterrupted internet access, while developing countries struggle with basic infrastructure, widening the digital divide.
MyNet Co. Public Relations Officer Christina Hughes promised enhanced safeguards, and several ISPs offered service credits and free upgrades without admitting legal liability.
